name: Tokio
summary: An asynchronous Rust runtime that combines task schedulers, an I/O event driver, timers, and asynchronous synchronization and networking utilities.

features.name: Bundled scheduler, driver, and timer services
features.description: Tokio's Runtime bundles a scheduler, an I/O event loop called the driver, and a timer service, and exposes construction and shutdown through one runtime type.
benefits: Presents the services needed by asynchronous applications behind one lifecycle boundary
Allows applications to configure runtime services together
costs: Runtime configuration couples task execution to resource-driver and timer choices
Applications must drive a runtime for tasks to make progress

features.name: Current-thread and work-stealing schedulers
features.description: Tokio provides a current-thread scheduler and a multi-thread scheduler. The multi-thread scheduler uses worker-local queues, a global queue, and work stealing; the current-thread scheduler executes tasks on one thread.
benefits: Supports lightweight single-thread deployments and parallel task execution
Makes scheduling strategy an explicit runtime configuration choice
costs: Different scheduler flavors expose different driving and Send constraints
Queue preference, stealing, and fairness behavior complicate latency reasoning

features.name: Readiness-driven task waking
features.description: The runtime checks I/O resources and timers, wakes tasks associated with ready events, and polls ready futures. The source separates driver readiness handling from scheduler task execution.
benefits: Lets many I/O-bound tasks share a bounded set of worker threads
Makes readiness and timer events explicit wakeup inputs
costs: A task that blocks a worker or fails to yield can delay unrelated work
Readiness, wakeups, and polling add coordination state to application reasoning

mathematical_views.question: How do I/O and timer readiness transitions move a future from waiting to scheduled polling?
assumptions: Tasks, resource registrations, and timer entries are state nodes
A readiness event produces a wakeup edge that makes a task eligible for polling
The view abstracts operating-system readiness APIs and future implementation details

mathematical_views.question: How do local queues, the global queue, lifo-slot behavior, and stealing determine which ready task is polled next?
assumptions: Each worker has a local queue and workers share a global injection queue
Queue operations and stealing are transitions over ready-task state
The model abstracts exact queue capacity, heuristics, and platform thread behavior

benefits: One lifecycle boundary for core async services
costs: Service configuration and runtime driving become coupled

benefits: Choice between local and parallel scheduling
costs: Scheduler-specific behavior complicates portability and latency analysis
Blocking work and wakeup coordination can delay progress
